title: An online shop for a skincare brand
metaTitle: A skincare shop built on ingredients
excerpt: Lead with ingredients, use, and restraint, then a short checkout. A skincare shop should not be a wall of claims or a marketplace of badges.
alt: A long, quiet office corridor with glass rooms, a teal sofa, and a dark kitchen. A skincare shop should feel this restrained: ingredients, use, and no wall of claims.
caption: A quiet corridor. The shop should feel this restrained. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a skincare product page lead with?
faqs.answer: The container, the size, the price, and one plain sentence about what it is, followed by ingredients and how to use it. Say who it is not for if you know. A headline that promises an overnight transformation does not tell anyone whether this is a wash or a cream.

faqs.question: How should subscriptions be offered?
faqs.answer: As an explicit choice, with the interval, the renewal price, and how to cancel visible before the first charge. Default to a one-time purchase. A preselected subscription is a future charge the buyer did not clearly choose, and it is hard to undo.

faqs.question: What claims should stay off the page?
faqs.answer: Ones you would not print on the carton. That includes borrowed clinical language, fear, fake scarcity, and before-and-after sliders that imply a guarantee. Reviews should be about the product named on the page, not a whole routine merged into one average.

markdown:
A skincare brand ecommerce website has to show what is in the bottle and how to use it, with restraint. The product page is not a wall of claims. Checkout is short, after the facts. A marketplace grid of badges, star bursts, and competing routines will make a careful brand look noisy, which is the opposite of what the product is selling.

Build the page around ingredients, use, and a photograph that does not shout. Leave the medical costume off unless you are prepared to defend it.

## Ingredients before adjectives

The first screen is the product, the size, and the price, with one sentence on what it is for. "A light moisturizer for dry skin" is a sentence. "Transform your barrier overnight" is a claim, and it does not tell anyone whether this is a wash, a cream, or an oil. Say the format in plain words.

Put the ingredient list in text, high enough that a buyer does not have to hunt, in an order you can stand behind. Allergens and the active you actually formulate around should be readable without a zoom. If a percentage matters, publish the percentage. If you will not publish it, do not hint at it with "potent dose" and a blur. Restraint is refusing the hint.

How to use it is a short method: when, how much, what to avoid combining if that is real. A twelve-step ritual that exists to sell the rest of the catalog is not a method. If the product works alone, say that it works alone. If it needs a sunscreen or a pause before another acid, say that, because silence there is how people have a bad week and blame the brand in public.

Who it is not for is part of restraint. Fragrance-sensitive, pregnancy, or a skin state you do not want using this: if you know, say so in a sentence. You are not their clinician. You are also not required to pretend the jar is for everyone. A clear exclusion prevents a bad review and a worse experience.

## Claims you can keep

Every adjective on the page should be one you would print on the carton and defend in a reply. "Fragrance free" if it is. "Unscented" only if you know the difference and mean it. "Clinically proven" only when there is a study you can describe without inflating it. If you cannot summarize the study in two sentences, do not wear the badge.

Before-and-after images are a claim. If you use them, the conditions, the time, and the fact that this is one person belong next to the image. A slider that implies a guaranteed week is a wall of claims even when the layout is minimal. Many small brands should skip the slider and show the texture of the product instead. Texture is honest. A promise of a new face is not.

Reviews, if you show them, are from people who used the product, with the product named. Do not merge reviews across a routine into a single product's average. Do not buy a paragraph. Google's guidance on [creating helpful, reliable people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) fits this page directly: write for a person trying to choose a bottle, and do not produce lines mainly to collect a search phrase. A page that repeats "best serum for glowing skin" in every heading is a wall of claims aimed at a robot. The buyer wanted the ingredient list.

Fear is a claim too. "Your skin is damaged without this" is pressure. Describe what the product is, and let them decide. A calm brand that panics in the template will feel incoherent, and incoherence is where trust dies in this category.

## A shelf of one brand

The collection uses one crop, one background, and type that can sit next to a pharmacy fact without shouting over it. Do not mix a splash of liquid, a model's cheek, and a bottle as three equal tiles. The bottle or the tube is the thumbnail. Texture and use live on the product page.

Routines can be a page when you truly mean a routine: which products, in which order, and the price of the set. Do not generate a routine page for every synonym of dry skin. Thin pages with the same three bottles and a new adjective are how a small catalog starts to look like a content mill. One honest concern page is better than ten.

Filters are useful when the line is long: format, or ingredient, or fragrance-free. They are not useful when you have six products. Six products need a quiet list and good type.

Samples and travel sizes need their own price and size, and the ingredient list should match the full size if it does. A sample that is a different formula is a different product. Say so, or do not sell it as a trial of the other.

## Checkout after the facts

The page did the explaining. Checkout collects email, address, shipping with a price, and payment. If a subscription exists, the interval, the renewal price, and how to cancel are visible before the first charge, not in a policy link only. A subscription is a second product. A single bottle should allow a guest. Baymard Institute's [cart abandonment research](https://baymard.com/lists/cart-abandonment-rate) found that 18 percent of US online shoppers had abandoned a cart because the site wanted an account, 17 percent because checkout was too long or complicated, and 19 percent because they did not trust the site with a card. The average documented abandonment rate in that compilation of 50 studies is 70.22 percent. Browsers are part of it: 42 percent said they were not ready to buy. The ready ones still leave when the path looks like a club they must join, or when the total appears late.

Extra costs are 40 percent in that study. Show shipping before the card. If you cannot ship a liquid to a region, say so on the product page. Discovering it after the routine has been built in the cart is a mess of claims and logistics.

Baymard's ideal checkout is about 12 to 14 form elements, or 7 to 8 fields, against a US average of 23.48 elements. You can be at the short end. Do not add a skin quiz as a gate in front of payment. A quiz can exist for people who want help. It is not the door to the buy button.

Use a payment provider a stranger can recognize, and say who processes the card. A new brand borrows trust from that sentence and from the calm of the ingredient list. It does not borrow trust from a padlock icon and a paragraph of superlatives.

## What you leave off

Leave off countdown timers, invented scarcity, and "only 2 left" on a cream you can fill again next week. Leave off a chat that diagnoses skin. A person can answer a question about the ingredient list. A bot should not tell someone to stop a prescription or start an acid. If you are not sure a question is yours to answer, the page should already contain the cautious sentence, and the reply should point to it.

Leave off autoplaying before-and-after. Leave off a pop-up discount before the ingredients have loaded. If you discount, show the price. A code that changes the meaning of "value" makes the calm page feel like a stall.

Do not collect more health information than you need to ship the order. A quiz that stores sensitive details is a different product with a different duty of care. If you do not have that duty handled, do not store it. The order needs an address. It does not need a medical history.

[Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services) include brand, ecommerce, and the front end for a catalog a small team can edit. When an ingredient changes, the list on the page has to change with it. That is a field, not a poster baked into an image, on a stack such as Next.js, React, and TypeScript.

## When the formula changes

Date the change internally. If the allergen or the active changes, update the page before the new batch ships, and write to recent buyers if the change would matter to them. The workflow can find the orders. A person writes the note. A generated "even better formula" letter is a claim. A letter that says what changed is a fact.

Keep the old list available to your support person so they can answer "I bought this in March" without guessing. The public page shows the current jar. The support note can say the previous one. Those are different documents. Mixing them on the product page will make both look untrustworthy.

Shade and scent variants, if they share a formula base, still get their own names and, when the look differs, their own photographs. A tinted and an untinted cream under one gallery will produce the wrong bathroom surprise.

## A quiet page on a phone

The first screen on a phone is the bottle, the price, the size, and the one-line what-it-is. Ingredients follow without a fight from a banner. Tap targets for a subscription versus a one-time purchase must be obvious, because that choice is about future charges. Default the choice to one-time unless they explicitly pick the repeat. A preselected subscription is a dark pattern dressed as convenience, and it is hard to undo once the charge repeats.

The photographs have to practice the same restraint as the copy. [Product photography for a skincare brand](/blog/product-photography-for-a-skincare-brand) is the next piece, because a loud crop, a different background per serum, and claims set in the image will undo the quiet page you just wrote.
